blocks.text: 0.7 grams of fat. Saturated fat is 0 grams, supporting a cleaner fat profile. For fruit, fat is usually just a small side note.

11.9 grams of carbs. Sugar is 4.4 grams, helping keep the sugar load under control. Fibre is 6.5 grams, helping with digestion and steadier meals. For fruit, the carb score mostly comes down to sugar control and fibre.
1.2 grams of protein. Not enough protein to be a real strength. For fruit, protein is usually too low to matter much.

Vitamin C is 31% daily value, useful for collagen formation and antioxidant support. Vitamin A is only 1% daily value, not bringing much vision or immune support. For fruit, vitamin C and vitamin A are usually the vitamin scores that matter most.

Magnesium is 5% daily value, the best number here but still too low to carry this section. Potassium is only 3% daily value, not bringing much fluid-balance support. For fruit, minerals are a bonus unless the numbers are unusually strong.

Positives first: anthocyanin-rich berry pigments. The red-purple pigment story adds a food-specific antioxidant angle. Fuller texture helps real meals. That practical fullness is one reason it can work beyond the numbers. Sweet role is easy to understand. It can be useful when sweetness is the job and the portion is deliberate.

Downsides next: very short shelf life. They spoil quickly, so waste and timing matter. Tiny seeds can bother some people. The seed texture is part of the fruit, but not everyone likes it. Price swings hard out of season. Fresh raspberries can become expensive compared with sturdier fruit.

Big strengths are fibre, vitamin C, and anthocyanin-rich berry pigments, but the biggest weaknesses are low potassium, low vitamin A, and low protein amount. It's good for heart health, digestion, and low-calorie flavour swaps because fibre is useful for heart health, fibre helps digestion and keeps meals steadier, and it adds flavour without adding many calories.
